transcript:
Fireflies.ai — Call Transcript

Meeting: OmniComply x Redwood — Security/Audit Review (Dedicated autoscaling + audit trail)
Date: 2026-01-15
Start time: 17:00 UTC
Duration: 47 minutes

Attendees
Redwood Inference: Liam O'Rourke (TAM), Rachel Kim (Customer Success), Marcus Lin (Security Eng), Kevin Osei (Security Eng), Jada Williams (Console/Platform)
OmniComply: Sarah Nguyen (GRC Lead), Daniel Brooks (Security Engineer), Priya Desai (Platform Eng Manager), Miguel Alvarez (Compliance Auditor)

---
Summary (auto-generated)
- OmniComply is evaluating Redwood Dedicated for regulated workloads.
- Main focus: audit trail and evidence for autoscaling decisions and configuration changes (min/max bounds), plus who changed what and when.
- Redwood discussed current and planned Console “Scaling History” and audit event logging, RBAC, and export options.
- Open questions: retention periods, SIEM integration, and semantics during maintenance/drains.

Topics (auto-generated)
1) Audit log requirements (scaling decisions vs config changes)
2) Dedicated autoscaling bounds (min/max) and enforcement
3) RBAC / SSO and admin actions
4) Audit log export + retention
5) Evidence collection for audit / reporting

---

[00:00] Liam O'Rourke: Alright, we’re at the top of the hour. Thanks everyone for joining. This is Liam, I’m the TAM on our side. We’ve got Rachel from Customer Success, Marcus and Kevin from security engineering, and Jada from Console. 

[00:12] Sarah Nguyen: Hi. Sarah here, GRC. Thanks for pulling the right folks in.

[00:16] Daniel Brooks: Daniel, security engineering.

[00:18] Priya Desai: Priya, platform. I’m the one who’d have to, uh, run this day to day.

[00:22] Miguel Alvarez: Miguel Alvarez. I’m supporting the audit workstream. I’ll probably ask annoying questions, sorry in advance.

[00:28] Rachel Kim: (laughs) No worries, that’s why we’re here.

[00:31] Liam O'Rourke: Cool. We saw the list of questions you sent over, specifically around autoscaling controls and audit evidence. Before we dive in, can you confirm the scope—this is for Dedicated pools, right? Not the hosted API.

[00:43] Sarah Nguyen: Correct. Dedicated capacity. And we’re particularly focused on autoscaling because that’s where spend and performance can surprise you. We need it to be bounded and we need an audit trail.

[00:56] Liam O'Rourke: Got it. Jada, do you want to frame what we log today vs what’s shipping shortly? 

[01:02] Jada Williams: Sure. So, two “audit” buckets to separate: (1) configuration change events—like someone updating min GPUs or max GPUs or cooldowns—and (2) operational scaling decisions—like “autoscaler chose desired=12, but clamped to max=10” with the reason. 

[01:19] Priya Desai: That’s exactly the separation we need. And for the config changes, we need who did it, what value changed from/to, and when. And ideally, from what IP or auth context. 

[01:33] Marcus Lin: Yep. For configuration changes, in our control plane we capture actor identity (user/service principal), timestamp, and the diff of the fields. IP can be present depending on auth path; for SSO/SAML we’ll have identity and session. For API tokens we store token id / client id and we recommend short-lived tokens.

[01:54] Miguel Alvarez: And, sorry, is that immutable? Like can an admin delete the logs?

[01:58] Marcus Lin: Admins can’t “edit” events. There is a retention policy, but the records aren’t user-editable. Internally we treat them like append-only. For export, we can push to your SIEM so you have independent storage.

[02:15] Sarah Nguyen: “Retention policy” is a loaded phrase. We need seven years for certain evidence. I’m guessing you don’t keep it that long in-product.

[02:25] Kevin Osei: In-product, no, we don’t do seven years by default. Typical retention is 30–90 days for high-volume operational events. Config change events can be longer, but seven years would be via export. That’s pretty standard.

[02:41] Daniel Brooks: Okay. For SIEM export, what are the supported routes? Splunk, Sentinel, S3…?

[02:49] Kevin Osei: Today: we support audit log export for control plane events via webhook and S3-compatible sink, depending on deployment mode. Splunk HEC is on the roadmap; for some customers we’ve used a webhook to a collector that forwards to Splunk. For private/VPC deployments, we can do it via your egress-controlled endpoint.

[03:12] Priya Desai: When you say “control plane events”—does that include autoscaling decisions? Like every scale up and down?

[03:19] Jada Williams: That’s the second bucket. Scaling decision events are higher volume, and also more nuanced on cardinality. We’re rolling out a “Scaling History” view in Console that’s backed by structured events. It includes the evaluated bounds and the decision inputs. Export is available but we need to be careful not to drown you with per-minute events if the pool is oscillating.

[03:45] Miguel Alvarez: Actually, we do want the decision history. If it’s an audit, we need evidence that the system respected a cap. Specifically: “max was 10; system never exceeded 10.”

[03:58] Marcus Lin: Understood. There are two ways to evidence that: (a) configuration evidence of max=10, plus (b) operational evidence that applied replicas never went above 10 and any attempted desire was clamped. 

[04:11] Daniel Brooks: So you log both desired and applied.

[04:14] Jada Williams: Yes. The event schema includes desired_replicas, applied_replicas, and clamp_reason. For example clamp_reason could be “customer_max_bound” or “fleet_capacity_shortage” or “rate_limit.” 

[04:28] Priya Desai: Wait—applied replicas could be lower due to fleet shortage? I thought Dedicated was… dedicated.

[04:34] Liam O'Rourke: It is dedicated capacity, but there are edge cases: maintenance, GPU replacement, region incident. We aim to honor your min, but there are semantics there—min is “best effort” during drains unless you’ve purchased a strict floor with capacity guarantees. 

[04:54] Sarah Nguyen: Let’s pause there. Our auditors are going to ask “what does min mean.” If you can’t guarantee min, we need the exception path fully logged.

[05:05] Marcus Lin: Totally. That’s where the decision events are helpful: if min is not satisfied, we log the reason code. Like “maintenance_drain” or “capacity_shortage” with incident id reference. Also, for config changes, we log who changed min/max and when.

[05:24] Miguel Alvarez: I want a clear statement. Is max hard? Like never exceed even if there’s demand.

[05:30] Jada Williams: Yes. Max is enforced as a hard clamp in the autoscaler. Meaning the controller will not apply above max. If demand exceeds, the system will throttle/queue and you’ll see it in metrics.

[05:44] Priya Desai: Good. And you’ll warn us in Console if we set max too low?

[05:49] Jada Williams: There are warnings and recommended settings. We also show “throttling due to max cap” so it’s obvious why latency might increase.

[06:00] Daniel Brooks: And the config change events—do they include changes made by Redwood support? Like if you guys do something on our behalf.

[06:07] Marcus Lin: Yes, that’s an important point. We distinguish Redwood operator actions versus customer admin actions. Redwood internal access is restricted and logged. If a Redwood employee changes configuration, that generates an audit event with an internal actor id and the ticket/incident reference. 

[06:25] Sarah Nguyen: That’s required. We have a policy that vendor admins must be attributable and reviewable.

[06:31] Rachel Kim: And operationally, we try to avoid making changes without an explicit customer request. But in emergencies we have break-glass; that’s also logged.

[06:41] Miguel Alvarez: Can your customer admins see those Redwood-internal change logs in the Console?

[06:47] Jada Williams: In the product, you’ll see that a change was made and the actor type (customer vs Redwood operator). For detailed internal notes we usually reference the ticket id you already have. For sensitive info we don’t expose everything, but the fact of the change is visible.

[07:07] Priya Desai: Okay. Let’s get concrete. We want to configure min and max. What’s the naming—min_replicas, min_gpus? 

[07:15] Jada Williams: In Dedicated we expose it as min_replicas and max_replicas at the pool level, and we map to GPUs behind the scenes depending on the serving topology. Some customers call it “min GPUs,” but the API field is replicas.

[07:31] Priya Desai: That’s already a potential audit gotcha. Our internal docs talk in GPUs. We’ll have to explain replicas.

[07:36] Liam O'Rourke: We can provide a mapping doc for your specific pool type, like 1 replica = 1 GPU node for your config, if that’s the case.

[07:45] Daniel Brooks: For audit, we just need consistency. If it’s replicas, fine.

[07:51] Sarah Nguyen: Back to audit logs. We need:
- who changed min/max and when
- what the values were before/after
- who approved (if you support approvals)
- scaling actions: when the system scaled and why
- evidence max was never exceeded

[08:09] Marcus Lin: We don’t have an “approval workflow” in-product yet, like four-eyes. But you can implement that via IAM—only a small group has write access, and you can require changes via your infrastructure pipeline. The audit trail will show which identity performed the change.

[08:26] Miguel Alvarez: That might be a control gap depending on their SOC controls.

[08:30] Sarah Nguyen: Not necessarily, we can manage change control ourselves, but we need the logs. We also need them exportable.

[08:38] Kevin Osei: Understood. For export: control plane config changes are already exportable; scaling decision events are in progress for export, currently visible in Console and available via API. We’re aligning the export to include them too.

[08:55] Daniel Brooks: Sorry, you said “available via API”—what kind of API? REST endpoint to query events?

[09:00] Jada Williams: Yes, a paginated endpoint like /dedicated/pools/{id}/scaling-events, filterable by time range and event type. You can pull and forward to your SIEM if needed.

[09:12] Priya Desai: That’s fine as long as it’s stable and we can backfill.

[09:16] Jada Williams: Exactly. We support pagination with cursors and a retention window. For long-term, you’d schedule a pull job.

[09:25] Sarah Nguyen: What about configuration audit log endpoint. Is it separate?

[09:29] Jada Williams: Yes, configuration events are in the broader audit log stream; scaling events are scoped to the pool.

[09:38] Miguel Alvarez: I want to understand the “why did we scale” details. Do you store raw signals? Like queue depth and p95 latency at that moment.

[09:46] Jada Williams: We store a snapshot of key inputs: queue depth, utilization, recent QPS/token rate estimate, throttles, and the evaluated policy outputs—cooldown state, rate limits, and bounds. We don’t store every raw timeseries sample; it’s a summary.

[10:05] Daniel Brooks: That’s okay. But be careful—if you store customer prompts or content in logs, that’s a no-go.

[10:11] Marcus Lin: We don’t log prompt content in these audit events. They’re operational metrics and ids. Content logging is separate and configurable.

[10:20] Priya Desai: On the “who changed it” question: do you support SSO so user identity is our corporate identity?

[10:27] Marcus Lin: Yes. SSO/SAML for Console access, SCIM for provisioning is available for enterprise. RBAC is role-based and you can scope pool admins vs viewers.

[10:39] Sarah Nguyen: And for API changes—like if we change min/max via Terraform or whatever—does it show as the service account name.

[10:47] Marcus Lin: Exactly. It’ll show as that token/client. We recommend separate tokens per pipeline so you can attribute.

[10:58] Miguel Alvarez: Can you demonstrate the evidence that max isn’t exceeded? Like a report.

[11:03] Rachel Kim: We can. There’s a metric and dashboard: applied_replicas for the pool, and an alert if applied > max (which should be impossible). We also track bound violations as an SLI—should be zero.

[11:19] Daniel Brooks: That alert helps. But from audit standpoint, you’d provide the dashboard export plus the event logs.

[11:25] Liam O'Rourke: Right, and we can include that as part of the security packet: what fields are logged, the SLI definitions, and how you can export.

[11:35] Priya Desai: I’ve got one more practical question. If we set max to 10 and demand spikes, what happens? Queueing? Throttling? Does it fail open by scaling past max?

[11:47] Jada Williams: It does not scale past max. It will queue up to configured queue depth, then return throttles. In Console you’ll see “throttle events” and the scaling history will show “desired=14, clamped to 10 due to customer_max_bound.”

[12:05] Sarah Nguyen: That’s good. But we need transparency. Our internal stakeholders will accuse the vendor if performance drops.

[12:12] Rachel Kim: Totally. That’s why we’re investing in the “why” fields.

[12:17] Miguel Alvarez: I’m going to ask a pedantic question: If Redwood changes default bounds in a migration, is that a config change event attributed to Redwood?

[12:26] Marcus Lin: Yes, migration/backfill jobs are service identities and logged, and if it changes your effective config, it’s in the audit record with the actor as “redwood-system” (or similar) and the change reason. We try to avoid changing customer semantics silently.

[12:45] Daniel Brooks: Do you have a concept of “evaluated config” vs “declared config”? Like defaults applied.

[12:51] Jada Williams: Yes. There’s “declared” config you set, and “evaluated/resolved” config after applying defaults and validation. The scaling decision event references the evaluated config so you can see what was actually used.

[13:06] Priya Desai: That matters. Cooldowns and rate limits too.

[13:10] Jada Williams: Exactly.

[13:13] Sarah Nguyen: Let’s talk about audit evidence collection. Miguel, what’s your checklist so we know we’re answering correctly?

[13:20] Miguel Alvarez: Sure. For this control area, we typically look for:
1) Access controls (RBAC/SSO)
2) Change management traceability (who/when/what)
3) Operational monitoring and anomaly response (alerts, runbooks)
4) Log retention and integrity
5) Export to customer-controlled archive

[13:39] Sarah Nguyen: And specifically for autoscaling, we need to show changes to bounds and the fact max was enforced.

[13:46] Kevin Osei: For integrity and retention, we can provide documentation of how audit logs are stored and protected. Also, we can discuss export with signing or checksums—depends on what you need.

[13:58] Daniel Brooks: Do you sign logs?

[14:00] Kevin Osei: We don’t currently provide cryptographic signing for every event as a product feature. But you can export to your own WORM storage or immutable bucket policies. Some customers do that.

[14:13] Miguel Alvarez: That’s acceptable if they have compensating controls.

[14:18] Priya Desai: Another question: If scaling decisions are “high volume,” do you ever sample them? Because for audit we need completeness.

[14:27] Jada Williams: We do not randomly sample away critical events. What we do is control volume by logging on decision boundaries—when desired changes, when a clamp happens, when cooldown prevents a change, etc. Not every loop iteration if nothing changes.

[14:47] Priya Desai: That’s fine. We don’t need no-op loops.

[14:51] Sarah Nguyen: And config changes are always logged.

[14:54] Marcus Lin: Correct.

[14:56] Liam O'Rourke: I want to make sure we cover “who changed max/min, when.” That’s the top item. Marcus, can you describe the fields in the change log entry in plain terms?

[15:08] Marcus Lin: Sure. Example:
- event_type: config.update
- resource: DedicatedPool/{pool_id}
- actor: sarah.nguyen@omnicomply.com (or service-account name)
- actor_type: user | service | redwood_operator
- timestamp
- change: min_replicas 4 -> 6; max_replicas 10 -> 12
- request_id / trace_id
And optionally a “reason” string if you provide it (like “planned product launch”).

[15:35] Sarah Nguyen: You said “reason string if you provide it.” Is there a field for change request id?

[15:41] Jada Williams: We can accept a client-provided annotation header in the API request that we store in the audit event. So you could pass your change ticket id.

[15:52] Priya Desai: That is huge. We can require our pipeline to attach Jira ticket.

[15:57] Daniel Brooks: As long as it’s not free-form from random users.

[16:01] Priya Desai: (laughs) It would come from our pipeline.

[16:05] Miguel Alvarez: Great. That helps evidence a lot.

[16:09] Sarah Nguyen: Okay. Switching gears slightly. We also need “audit trail of scaling decisions.” What does that look like?

[16:17] Jada Williams: For scaling decisions, an event might be:
- event_type: autoscaler.decision
- pool_id
- computed_desired
- applied
- bounds: min, max
- clamp_reason: none | customer_max_bound | customer_min_bound | rate_limit | cooldown | capacity_shortage
- input_summary: queue_depth, utilization, p95_latency, throttle_rate
- optional: forecast value + confidence (if predictive scaling is enabled)

[16:48] Daniel Brooks: You mentioned forecast. Is that on now?

[16:51] Liam O'Rourke: It’s coming in phases. For you, since you’re evaluating, we can keep predictive off and use reactive scaling plus bounds. But the audit schema supports it.

[17:02] Sarah Nguyen: For the audit itself, we don’t necessarily need forecast, we need reproducibility and explainability.

[17:08] Miguel Alvarez: Exactly. In an audit, “model said so” is not a good explanation.

[17:13] Jada Williams: Understood. That’s why we include confidence gating and fallbacks. But again, we can focus on bounded reactive for initial rollout.

[17:24] Priya Desai: I’m going to ask about Console access logs. Do you log logins and access to the scaling history page?

[17:31] Marcus Lin: We log authentication events and administrative actions. Viewing a page is not always logged as an audit event; depends on the sensitivity. For some enterprise plans we do “data access” logs for certain resources. We can confirm what’s available for your tier.

[17:51] Sarah Nguyen: For compliance, admin actions matter more than viewing, but viewing could matter if it’s sensitive. Scaling history isn’t that sensitive.

[18:00] Daniel Brooks: Agree.

[18:02] Liam O'Rourke: Okay. Are there any procurement/legal style requirements like data residency for audit logs? 

[18:08] Sarah Nguyen: Yes. We prefer US regions only. For audit exports, we need to know where they land.

[18:14] Kevin Osei: For Dedicated, we can keep control plane and log storage in region according to your deployment configuration. For export to your S3, it’s wherever your bucket is.

[18:29] Priya Desai: One more: if our pool is multi-region, how do logs work? Are scaling events per-region?

[18:36] Jada Williams: Scaling is per pool but the events include region dimension if the pool spans regions. It can get complex; for the first deployment we usually recommend single-region Dedicated pools for compliance reasons.

[18:52] Daniel Brooks: Good. That simplifies.

[18:55] Sarah Nguyen: I think we’ve hit most of it. Miguel, anything else?

[19:00] Miguel Alvarez: Two items:
1) demonstrate that audit events themselves are protected from tampering
2) confirm what happens during maintenance with min bound. If min is “best effort,” we need documented exceptions.

[19:15] Marcus Lin: For tampering: internal permissions are restricted, and exports are recommended for your own immutability controls. For min semantics: we will provide the documented behavior—min is enforced by autoscaler, but can be temporarily violated during node drain/maintenance or hard capacity incident; those are logged with reason codes.

[19:36] Priya Desai: That’s okay as long as it’s rare and visible.

[19:40] Rachel Kim: And we can set alerts on “below min” duration so you get paged if it happens.

[19:47] Daniel Brooks: Great.

[19:49] Sarah Nguyen: Can you send us sample log entries? Like sanitized JSON.

[19:55] Jada Williams: Yes, we can send examples of both types: config.update and autoscaler.decision.

[20:03] Liam O'Rourke: We’ll do that. Also, we can schedule a short follow-up where Jada shares the Console screens for Scaling History and config audit views.

[20:12] Priya Desai: Please. Seeing it will help.

[20:15] Sarah Nguyen: Alright, recap next steps?

[20:18] Liam O'Rourke: Yep.
- We’ll send the audit event schema/examples, including fields for who/when and scaling decision reasons.
- Kevin will confirm export options for scaling events and what’s GA vs roadmap.
- Marcus will send a statement on log integrity and Redwood operator actions visibility.
- You’ll confirm required retention and SIEM requirements.
Then we’ll schedule a demo of the Scaling History view.

[20:46] Sarah Nguyen: Works.

[20:48] Miguel Alvarez: Thanks everyone.

[20:49] Daniel Brooks: Thanks.

[20:50] Priya Desai: Thank you.

[20:52] Liam O'Rourke: Great. Ending the recording.

---
Questions (auto-generated)
- Does Redwood cryptographically sign audit logs? (Answer: not per-event signing as a product feature today; recommend customer export to immutable storage.)
- Are autoscaling max bounds a hard cap? (Answer: yes, enforced; system will throttle/queue instead of exceeding max.)
- Are min bounds guaranteed during maintenance? (Answer: generally enforced, but may be temporarily violated during drains/maintenance/capacity incidents with reason codes logged.)

End of transcript
